primitives.name: Spectral Prediction Kernel
primitives.verbatim_quote: Method / model Hilbert-space prediction theory: a stationary (second-order) continuous-time process X is represented spectrally (CR), mapped to L2 of its spectral measure (KIT), given a moving-average representation driven by orthogonal-increment noise (MA), and prediction reduces to orthogonal projection onto the closed linear span of the observed past.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'X(t)': 'stochastic process, dimensionless', 'c*(t-u)': 'prediction kernel, time-dimensioned', 'W(u)': 'orthogonal increment noise, dimensionless'}
primitives.assumptions: Second-order stationarity, Szegő condition, Gaussianity for white noise interpretation.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Non-stationary or non-Gaussian processes invalidate the spectral decomposition.

layer2.mapping: Maps spectral density estimate to prediction kernel via inverse Fourier transform; used in GSE for continuous-time signal extrapolation.
layer2.telemetry: RMSE between predicted and actual trajectory over short horizons.

reasoning_traces.think:
The paper formalizes continuous-time prediction within a Hilbert-space framework, leveraging the Cramér representation (CR) to map stochastic processes into L2 spaces defined by their spectral measures. This allows for orthogonal projections onto subspaces generated by past observations, yielding a moving-average (MA) representation driven by orthogonal increments. The core innovation lies in streamlined proofs of Wiener-Kolmogorov-Krein theorems using Doob’s method, but without empirical validation or estimation procedures. As such, the framework assumes known spectral densities and prediction kernels, which are typically estimated in practice—rendering it unsuitable for direct GSE implementation. However, its structure supports nonparametric spectral predictors that could be evaluated against discrete-time Kalman filters on short-horizon NFL tracking data. The failure mode arises from non-stationarity and lack of estimation methodology, which are critical in real-world applications.
